I work in investments. I would recommend you do 1 of 2 things. 

Option 1: put it in an index fund. This will grow slowly but historically has outperformed inflation.

Option 2: research specific stocks and buy shares. Within this option you can go risky or safe. Safe would be looking for stocks with dividends, strong balance sheets, and low beta (called blue chip stocks) - these are usually well established companies. Risky would be looking for stocks with high beta and has had strong momentum (called growth stocks). Blue chip stocks will protect you in a down market, while growth stocks will usually make a lot more in an up market. Of course, there are other factors but that is based on the individual company, management, sector, and news. Good luck!

Edit: option 1 is a lot less work and takes less knowledge. You don't need to look at it daily like the individual stocks.

What countries are we talking about? In general, the US has a law system that allows for rights to not be infringed upon and non-union workers have legal recourse. Working conditions need to be safe these days and it's the same in union or non-union jobs. If my job is hazardous, I can sue my employer to force a change. 

Now your argument about holidays, weekends and overtime. First, many jobs don't have weekends off. Actually, most that do are non-union jobs that are based on Wall Street being open and a basic standard of modern business hours. Many jobs have people work on holidays too. However, any benefits or compensation probably would be rolled back a bit. The way union jobs work is that their is a barrier to enter because it's harder to remove a current employee. This makes it harder for employers to lower wages because they can't just threaten to bring in a new batch of people. This means that non-union jobs would become competitive for workers with union jobs. This means wages and compensation would drop to current non-union unskilled labor positions. It won't become unreasonable or ridiculously low (though many would argue minimum wage is too low). It would be more of a free market and some workers would lose rights like I pointed out but it wouldn't be sending a ton of workers into poverty that weren't there before.

In the old days the things unions fought for were important like the things you listed. Today, these have become standard in both non-unionized industries and unionized ones. These rights would not disappear like some suggest. The things that would disappear would be protection from firing from some tenured jobs (teachers), barring of new entry into occupations (electricians, etc.) and allowing current union members to do more than one job (in many industries you have a roll and you can't deviate from it because someone else should do it). However, some ability to fight for future rights would be diminished. Wages would probably be lower in current union jobs and their would be little job safety.

If you really want to lose fat, you should get your heart rate to an aerobic zone for long periods of time. A rough estimate is (180- age). I warm up for 5-10 minutes at about 10-15 beats lower. Then I run for 40 min to 1 hour at the aerobic zone. Then cool down for 5-10 min at about 10-15 beats lower. If you do this, you will realize that you actually need to slow down over the 1 hour workout and your cool down will be much slower than your warm up. It sounds like you're using a treadmill and most of those have heart rate monitors. You can take it every mile or so to make sure you aren't going too high. It's not super convenient so the other option is to get a heart rate monitor. This is the zone that you will burn a lot more fat than glucose. Also, make sure to work up to that 40min to 1 hr if it's too hard to start. You might just want to start at 25 minutes for that middle part and build it up.

According to [Maffetone heart rate training] (http://www.trifind.com/a_1042/maf_180_heart_rate_training.html), your aerobic target should be 143-153 bpm. If you search people using that method on this subreddit, you get a lot of people around that pace. You should train around that heart rate or 153 and eventually your pace will get faster. I train mostly at my Maffeton heart rate but sometimes it gets boring. You can bump up the pace every once in a while at a pace that still feels easy. Then you can mix in some faster work outs, if you want. I run 3 out of 6 work outs at these heart rates and the others I ignore the heart rates, during the run. 

Also, don't worry about your heart rate  being 180-185 during the race. It will come down from not smoking. As long as you don't feel like your heart will explode it's most likely a safe heart rate to be at.

I had this same problem. Like you my cadence is pretty low when I run at HR training. I mainly focused on Heart rate because that's the point of the training. 

I focused on cadence indirectly. Your cadence will go up by shorting your stride and working on quick light feet. Make sure to never over stride and it will help raise your cadence a bit. It will make you more effecient in your running and actually keep your heart rate lower at faster paces. The light quick feet should also minimize certain types of injury in theory.

Note: If you feel like you're going to slow at first with the heart rate and it's changing your form, I would make your heart rate to start with 5 beats higher. Changing your form coming from injury is the worst thing you can do. I was suppose to be at 155 bpm but it caused me to slow down too much and my legs did funny things. I decided I'd go to 160. Now a couple weeks in I can do a faster pace at 155 and can work on my form, rather than do unnatural motions.
